t: The national security exception has no real standard
o: “Primary function” and “national security” are not defined. The president simply determines it.
u: The VA, the EPA, the FDA, the Weather Service and NASA were all declared to have a primary function of national security work.
f: Define national security work narrowly. Require a written finding for each unit. Bar the exclusion of whole departments.

t: Courts are told to assume the president got it right
o: A 1989 ruling gives exclusion orders a “presumption of regularity.”
u: Appeals courts lifted injunctions even where trial judges had found the order was likely retaliation.
f: Give federal courts fresh review of the facts and the law, with the burden on the government and no presumption.

t: There is no process and no role for Congress
o: No notice, no comment period, no waiting period, no report to Congress.
u: The March 2025 order was signed with no public notice and announced late at night. Agencies were told that same night they no longer had to bargain.
f: Send every order to Congress with its supporting facts. It takes effect only if Congress approves, and it expires after four years.

t: Nothing stops a president from playing favorites
o: The law does not bar an exclusion aimed at unions that criticize or sue the administration.
u: Police, firefighters and the Border Patrol kept their rights. VA spared smaller unions it said had caused little trouble.
f: Bar any exclusion based on a union's speech, lawsuits, grievances or politics, or one that treats similar workers differently.

t: The power can be handed down
o: Nothing stops a president from delegating the exclusion power to a cabinet secretary.
u: The March 2025 order let the Transportation Secretary exclude any part of the department, including the FAA, and let the Defense and VA secretaries decide which of their units get rights back.
f: The authority may not be delegated. If it is used, the president signs it and Congress votes on it.

t: Overseas posts and the Foreign Service have twin loopholes
o: A second clause lets the president suspend the law at any installation outside the 50 states, and the Foreign Service law copies the whole exception.
u: The March 2025 order used the Foreign Service version to exclude most of the State Department and USAID.
f: Apply every limit in the rewritten section 7103(b) to both.

t: Whole workforces sit outside the law
o: TSA officers and VA medical professionals are covered by separate statutes with weaker protections.
u: A single cabinet secretary ended bargaining for about 47,000 TSA officers in March 2025, and tried again in December after a court blocked it.
f: Bring TSA officers under this chapter. Narrow the Title 38 exclusions at VA.

t: Jobs can be defined out of the union
o: Managers, “confidential” employees, personnel staff, investigators and anyone doing security work are barred from bargaining units, and the labels are elastic.
u: Schedule F in 2020 and its 2025 successor were built to move career employees into categories with fewer protections. The job-by-job security exclusion in this section was passed over in 2025 in favor of excluding whole departments.
f: Tighten the definitions. A change in job category does not change unit status without a finding by the labor board or a court. Make the job-by-job security exclusion the normal route.

t: Congress can be talked into carving out whole departments
o: Nothing in Chapter 71 protects it from being waived by a later personnel bill.
u: After September 11, Congress let Homeland Security and the Pentagon write their own labor rules. The Homeland Security version let managers cancel signed contracts, and a unanimous appeals court said it made collective bargaining meaningless. The Pentagon's version, NSPS, survived in court and took an act of Congress to repeal in 2009.
f: State in the chapter that no personnel system may waive or modify it unless a later law says so in express terms, and require any such system to keep binding agreements and neutral review.

t: Management rights can swallow the rule
o: Mission, budget, organization, hiring, assignment, discipline and contracting out are all reserved to management. How far that reaches depends on who sits on the labor board.
u: The board's tests for when a union proposal interferes with a management right have changed with its majority.
f: Write into the statute that procedures and arrangements for affected employees are negotiable even when they touch a management right.

t: A whole category of bargaining switches on and off by executive order
o: Staffing levels, technology and methods of work are negotiable only “at the election of the agency.”
u: Clinton told agencies to bargain these subjects. Bush revoked that. Trump's 2018 order barred it. Biden restored it in 2021.
f: Make these subjects mandatory, or let a neutral decide when an agency refuses.

t: Pay and most benefits are off the table
o: Anything specifically provided for by federal statute is not a condition of employment. For most employees that removes pay, health insurance and retirement.
u: Opponents then argue that unions with so little to bargain exist only to obstruct.
f: Keep pay with Congress, and allow bargaining wherever an agency has discretion over pay, bonuses or schedules.

t: Government-wide rules override the bargaining table
o: A proposal that conflicts with a government-wide rule is not negotiable, so OPM or the president can remove a subject by issuing a rule.
u: The 2018 orders and OPM's follow-on rules were written to take discipline procedures and official time off the table everywhere at once.
f: Only a statute, or a rule a neutral finds is backed by compelling need, can limit bargaining. No rule overrides an agreement already in force.

t: The duty to bargain shifts with the labor board's majority
o: The statute does not say how big a change must be before an agency has to bargain, or whether bargaining continues during the life of a contract.
u: In 2020 the board issued its first policy statements in 35 years, raising the threshold to “substantial impact” and letting agencies demand an end to mid-contract bargaining. A federal appeals court threw both out in 2022 as poorly reasoned.
f: Put the long-standing rules in the statute: bargaining over any change that is more than trivial, and a continuing duty during the term of a contract.

t: Agency heads get a veto over signed contracts
o: The head of the agency has 30 days to disapprove an agreement the agency's own negotiators signed.
u: Administrations have used that review to strike provisions the White House disliked, including agreements signed in the last days of a prior administration.
f: Limit disapproval to a specific conflict with a statute, stated in writing, with fast review by a neutral.

t: Executive orders can dictate what gets bargained
o: Nothing stops a president from telling every agency what positions to take at the table.
u: The 2018 orders set bargaining positions for the whole government. In 2025, directives sought to void telework provisions in signed contracts.
f: No executive order or OPM guidance may narrow the duty to bargain or void an agreement during its term.

t: Board members can now be fired at will
o: The statute protects members from removal except for cause. In June 2026 the Supreme Court held that kind of protection unconstitutional at a similar agency.
u: The board's chair was fired without cause in February 2025, the first such removal in its history.
f: Stop depending on the board's independence. Give unions a path to court whenever the board is deadlocked, short a quorum, or will not act.

t: One official decides whether any violation is prosecuted
o: Only the General Counsel can issue an unfair labor practice complaint. The president can remove the General Counsel at any time, and a refusal to prosecute cannot be appealed.
u: The seat has had no Senate-confirmed occupant since 2017. With no one to issue complaints, charges pile up and nothing happens.
f: A career deputy acts automatically during a vacancy. Regional directors can issue complaints. If a charge is not acted on within 120 days, the union can sue.

t: The Impasses Panel belongs to the president
o: When bargaining deadlocks, a panel appointed by the president and removable by the president imposes the contract terms. Its decisions cannot be appealed directly.
u: A panel named by one administration can write management's proposals into contracts across the government, and the next administration can dismiss the whole panel and start over.
f: Send impasses to neutral arbitrators chosen by the parties from a federal mediation roster, with a written decision a court can review.

t: No deadlines, and fewer judges
o: Nothing requires the board to decide a case within any period.
u: Cases have waited years. In 2025 the board moved to eliminate its administrative law judges.
f: Set a deadline for each stage. If the board misses one, the decision below becomes final.

t: Breaking the law costs an agency nothing
o: The remedy for an unfair labor practice is an order to stop and a notice on the bulletin board. No fines and no damages.
u: An agency can repudiate a contract, wait out years of litigation, and at worst be told to post a notice.
f: Civil penalties for willful violations. Full make-whole relief for employees and unions, including lost dues, interest and attorney fees.

t: The penalties run one way
o: A union that strikes loses its recognition, and its members can be fired and prosecuted. An official who orders an agency to break this law faces nothing.
u: PATCO was decertified 80 days after its strike began. Nothing in the chapter penalizes the officials who cancelled contracts in 2025.
f: Make a willful violation of this chapter a prohibited personnel practice, with discipline for the official who ordered it.

t: Only the board can ask a court to stop a violation
o: A union cannot seek an injunction. Only the board can, and only after a complaint has issued.
u: With no General Counsel to issue complaints, the one emergency tool in the statute cannot be used.
f: Let unions seek injunctions directly. Require the board to seek one whenever an agency repudiates a contract or withdraws recognition.

t: The forum trap
o: A 2019 ruling sends unions to the labor board before they can go to court. A union that has been excluded from the law cannot use the labor board.
u: Unions spent months arguing over which courthouse door was open while their contracts were being cancelled.
f: Give federal district courts clear jurisdiction over challenges to exclusion orders and government-wide labor directives.

t: The board's orders do not enforce themselves
o: If an agency ignores an order, the board has to go to a court of appeals and ask for enforcement.
u: Delay is free. Every month of noncompliance is a month the agency gets what it wanted.
f: An order takes effect after 30 days unless a court stays it, and noncompliance is punishable as contempt.

t: Nothing holds the status quo in place
o: No rule stops an agency from acting first and litigating later.
u: In 2025, contracts covering hundreds of thousands of workers were cancelled mid-term, grievances were dropped and dues deductions were shut off while the lawsuits were still being argued.
f: No unilateral change while bargaining, an impasse or an appeal is pending. Agreements, pending cases and dues withholding stay in force until a final judgment.

t: Agencies can refuse to arbitrate
o: The statute requires a grievance procedure ending in binding arbitration but gives a union no way to make an agency show up.
u: In 2025 agencies including the VA stopped processing grievances and declined to take part in arbitration.
f: Let a union go to federal court for an order compelling arbitration, as private-sector unions can.

t: The board can overturn an arbitrator, and no court can review it
o: Either side can appeal an arbitrator's award to the board. Most of those rulings are final and cannot be taken to court.
u: A board majority hostile to an award can erase it, and the delay alone rewards the agency.
f: Write a deferential standard for arbitrators into the statute, allow court review, and require compliance while an appeal is pending.

t: Subjects can be pulled out of the grievance process
o: Some matters are excluded by statute, and administrations have pushed to exclude more.
u: The 2018 orders pressed agencies to keep removals and other actions out of grievance procedures.
f: Fix the list of exclusions in the statute and bar agencies from demanding more as a condition of agreement.

t: Official time can be squeezed by order
o: The statute guarantees official time for bargaining and leaves the rest to agreement, which an order can then restrict.
u: The 2018 orders capped official time across the government and barred its use for grievances.
f: Lock the official time provisions against limits imposed by executive order or guidance.

t: Dues withholding can be shut off
o: Payroll deduction of dues depends on the agency continuing to honor it.
u: Dues withholding was shut off across excluded agencies in 2025.
f: Require agencies to honor dues allotments until a court finally rules that a unit is outside the law.

t: Unions can be evicted and cut off
o: Office space, equipment and access to employees depend on what an agency is willing to agree to.
u: The 2018 orders ended unions' free use of government office space and equipment.
f: Guarantee reasonable access to the workplace, to employees and to the information a union needs to represent them.

t: The purpose clause is used against the purpose
o: The chapter says it should be read consistently with “an effective and efficient Government.”
u: That phrase is cited to resolve doubtful questions in management's favor.
f: Add a rule of construction: the chapter is to be read broadly to protect the right to bargain.
